I've been farming these 10.1 mu in Quzhou for 35 years. I'm 58 now, and my body doesn't handle the heavy labor like it used to. My son works off-farm at a factory in town, so it's mostly me and my wife managing the fields day-to-day. With only two of us, I have to be smart about labor. That's why I'll keep 7.5 mu in my wheat-maize rotation—that's our food security, and the harvest is mechanized. The remaining 2.6 mu I'll plant cotton for cash income, but I won't expand it because cotton picking in autumn still falls on us, and 2.6 mu is already plenty for our hands.

For wheat, I know this land well. I'll rotary till after the maize comes off and sow my usual improved winter wheat variety in October. I've learned over the years that throwing more nitrogen doesn't help—it just makes the wheat lodge when the spring winds come. So I'll apply about 16 kg of nitrogen per mu, along with phosphate and some potash. From my well I'll irrigate three times: once before winter to protect the seedlings, once at jointing in spring, and once at heading. Two pesticide sprays will keep the aphids and diseases in check. If the weather treats us fair, I should get around 500 kg per mu.

For summer maize, timing is everything. The season is short after wheat harvest in June, so I'll sow hybrid seed right away using the no-tillage seeder—no time to plough. Maize is a bit less demanding than wheat on fertilizer; I'll put down about 15 kg nitrogen per mu. I'll irrigate twice, at jointing and when it tassels, because summer rain can be unpredictable. Two sprays for armyworm and leaf diseases. I expect about 550 kg per mu.

For cotton, I'll deep plough that 2.6 mu plot in early spring—cotton likes a loose, deep seedbed. I'll plant an improved variety. Cotton needs more potassium for the bolls, so I'll apply a bit more potash than on the grains. I'll irrigate twice, at flowering and during boll filling. Three pesticide applications for bollworm—can't skip those. I'm hoping for 280 kg of seed cotton per mu, which should give us decent cash after costs.
